title: The three financial statements
objectives: Answer out loud: Walk me through the three statements.
Answer out loud: Why do we need a cash flow statement?
Answer out loud: Which statement matters most?

steps.heading: Income statement
steps.body: revenue, expenses, and profit over a *period*. Ends in net income.

steps.heading: Balance sheet
steps.body: what the company owns (assets), owes (liabilities), and what's left for owners (equity), at a *point in time*. Assets = Liabilities + Equity.

steps.heading: Cash flow statement
steps.body: reconciles net income to the actual change in cash. Three sections — operating, investing, financing.
The IS uses **accrual accounting**: revenue when earned, expenses when incurred — not when cash moves. The CFS exists to bridge that gap.

blocks.title: If you could only use one statement to judge a company, which?
blocks.teaser: The cash flow statement — it shows whether the business actually generates cash, which is what keeps it alive.
blocks.body:
The cash flow statement — it shows whether the business actually generates cash, which is what keeps it alive. With two statements, pick the BS and IS: you can rebuild the CFS from two balance sheets and an income statement.

**Interview answer:** "The cash flow statement, because cash is what keeps a company solvent. With two, the balance sheet and income statement, since you can derive the cash flow statement from them."

blocks.title: Why isn't net income the same as cash flow?
blocks.teaser: Three reasons: (1) non-cash expenses like D&A and stock-based comp reduce net income without using cash; (2) working capital — revenue on credit incr…
blocks.body:
Three reasons: (1) non-cash expenses like D&A and stock-based comp reduce net income without using cash; (2) working capital — revenue on credit increases net income before cash arrives; (3) some cash uses never hit the IS: CapEx, debt principal, dividends.

**Interview answer:** "Non-cash charges, working capital timing, and items like CapEx and debt repayment that skip the income statement."

blocks.prompt: Which of these is NOT a reason net income differs from cash flow?

options.text: Non-cash expenses like D&A and SBC
Working capital timing, like sales made on credit
Cash uses that skip the IS, like CapEx and debt principal
Revenue is recorded when cash is received

blocks.explanation: Under accrual accounting, revenue is recorded when earned, not when cash arrives — that mismatch is exactly why the CFS exists.

blocks.title: Examples of items on the IS but not the CFS, and vice versa?
blocks.teaser: IS but not cash: D&A, stock-based comp, impairments, unrealized gains.
blocks.body: IS but not cash: D&A, stock-based comp, impairments, unrealized gains. Cash but not IS: CapEx, buying inventory, issuing or repaying debt principal, dividends, share buybacks.

blocks.title: Where do dividends show up?
blocks.body:
Not on the income statement. They're paid from net income, so they reduce retained earnings on the balance sheet and appear as a financing outflow on the CFS. *Preferred* dividends are subtracted to get net income available to common shareholders.

**Interview answer:** "Dividends aren't an expense. They hit retained earnings and the financing section of the cash flow statement."

blocks.title: Accrual vs. cash accounting — give an example.
blocks.teaser: A software company bills $1,200 upfront for a 12-month subscription.
blocks.body: A software company bills $1,200 upfront for a 12-month subscription. Cash basis: $1,200 of revenue in month one. Accrual basis: $100 of revenue each month, with the unearned remainder sitting in deferred revenue (a liability).
